Detection of genomic sequences in microbial genomes by whole genome sequencing

section.content: 一种以读数形式检测微生物的测序的基因组中预定位置处的靶基因组序列的方法。所述方法包括计算靶基因组序列邻域位置中基因组的局部测序深度，所述计算包括以下步骤：a)在读数中检测来自所述微生物的至少一个参考基因组的一组数字基因组序列，b)生成第三组数字基因组序列，其包含读数和属于邻域的第二组数字基因组序列，c)计数第三组数字基因组序列中每个数字基因组序列的拷贝数，以及d)计算局部测序深度等于计数的拷贝数的最大值。

A method of detecting a target genomic sequence at a predetermined location in a sequenced genome of a microorganism in the form of a read. The method comprises calculating a local sequencing depth of a genome in a target genome sequence neighborhood position, the calculating comprising the steps of: a) detecting in the reads a set of digital genomic sequences from at least one reference genome of the microorganism, b) generating a third set of digital genomic sequences comprising the reads and a second set of digital genomic sequences belonging to a neighborhood, c) counting the copy number of each digital genomic sequence in the third set of digital genomic sequences, and d) calculating a local sequencing depth equal to the maximum of the counted copy numbers.

Detection of genomic sequences in microbial genomes by whole genome sequencingTechnical Field

The present invention relates to the field of microbial molecular analysis, and in particular to the identification of genomic sequences in sequenced genomes using whole genome sequencing techniques.

Advantageously, the invention is applicable to the identification of subspecies classification units to which the clonal complex of a microorganism, such as SARS-COVID-2 virus, belongs.

Background

Next generation (whole genome or targeted) sequencing ("NGS"), such as sequencing by the Illumina and Oxford Nanopore Technologies platform, greatly alters microbiological analysis of patient, food, or environmental samples by crossing common microbiological analysis workflow defects (e.g., low level of invasiveness to microorganisms in the sample, workflow duration or workflow complexity, etc.). If NGS technology shows many advantages, however, it requires a complex bioinformatics pipeline to process the reads generated by the sequencing platform. In fact, in general, pipelines rely on specific genomic sequence detection, such as determining the identity of a viral clone complex or bacterial antibiotic susceptibility, which can be a challenging task, as the genomic sequence may not be so present in a read or due to high sequencing error rates.

To confirm the presence of a particular sequence in a genome, one natural approach is to first calculate the copy number of the sequence in the reads and the average sequencing depth of the genome, and then conclude that the sequence is present if the copy number of the sequence exceeds a predetermined fraction of the average sequencing depth, as described in patent applications WO2021180771 and WO 2021180768. The concept behind such a pipeline relies on the fact that: if the number of copies of a particular sequence is found to be limited compared to the total number of sequences generated by the sequencing platform, it means that the copies are from sequencing errors. It can thus be concluded that the specific sequence is not actually present in the genome.

However, in addition to the variation of sequencing depth from genome to genome due to the WGS technique itself, an enrichment step aimed at increasing the number of certain genome parts may also be performed prior to the sequencing step. For example, in SARS-CoV2 variant identification, sequencing typically occurs after a preliminary step of genome amplification by large-scale multiplex PCR. Thus, the sequencing depth may vary greatly from genome to genome. On the one hand, if the actual sequencing depth of the target sequence position in the genome is well below the average depth, the pipeline is likely to give false negative results. On the other hand, if the actual sequencing depth of the target sequence position in the genome is much higher than the average depth, the pipeline is likely to give false positive results.

Disclosure of Invention

It is an object of the present invention to provide a robust method for detecting a specific genomic sequence (hereinafter referred to as "target genomic sequence") in a microbial genome in a set of reads generated by a aNGS workflow, even in the event of high variations in sequencing depth.

To this end, an object of the present invention relates to a method for detecting a target genomic sequence at a predetermined position in a genome of a microorganism, comprising:

-preparing a sample comprising at least one copy of the genome of the microorganism;

-sequencing the sample to generate a first set of digital genome sequences corresponding to the microbial genome;

-and for each target genomic sequence, the computer performs the steps of:

A. calculating a local sequencing depth of the microbial genome in the vicinity of the location of the target genomic sequence;

B. if the copy number of the target genomic sequence is above a predetermined fraction of the calculated local sequencing depth,

Detecting the presence of said target genomic sequence in the genome of said microorganism,

Wherein the step of calculating the local sequencing depth comprises the steps of:

A1. Detecting a second set of digital genomic sequences in the first set of digital genomic sequences, the second set comprising digital genomic sequences from at least one reference genome of the microorganism;

A2. generating a third set of digital genomic sequences comprising:

i. a first set of digital genomic sequences belonging to a neighborhood of the location of the target genomic sequence;

a second set of digital genomic sequences belonging to a neighborhood of said position of said target genomic sequence;

A3. counting the copy number of each digital genome sequence in the third set of digital genome sequences; and

A4. the local sequencing depth was calculated to be equal to the maximum of the counted copy numbers.

Microorganisms in the sense of the present invention mean viruses, bacteria, yeasts or fungi. In the sense of the present invention, the genome of a bacterium, yeast or fungus comprises both chromosomal and plasmid portions.

In other words, the detection according to the invention relies on the synergy of the following concepts:

i. If the copy number of the target genomic sequence in the read exceeds a fraction of the local sequencing depth, the presence of the target genomic sequence in the microbial genome is confirmed. By doing so, variations with actual sequencing depth of the genome are considered, thereby reducing the false positive rate and false negative rate observed when using average sequencing depth;

the estimation of the local sequencing depth depends on the count of target genomic sequences in the reads, as well as on the count of other target genomic sequences in their neighborhoods, and possibly of similar genomic sequences from target genomic sequence mutations observed in the microbial genome. The estimate of local sequencing depth is ultimately defined as the highest count found in the neighborhood of the target sequence, which reflects the actual composition of the organism's genome at the target sequence location more strongly than the average sequencing depth of the entire genome.

Furthermore, due to sequencing errors, the counts may not perfectly reflect the actual local sequencing depth. Thus, if a target sequence is not the most abundant sequence in its neighborhood, it cannot be said that the target sequence is not present in the genome only. By using the score of the estimated local sequencing depth, and thus the score of the most abundant sequence in the neighborhood of the target sequence, sequencing errors can be explicitly taken into account. Attention is paid here to the synergistic relationship between the local sequencing depth and the consideration of the error rate, since the latter cannot be managed without first defining the local sequencing depth.

According to one embodiment of the invention, the target genomic sequence is a k-mer, which is a constituent of variables of the model for predicting that the microorganism belongs to the clonal complex. In particular, the microorganism is a coronavirus and the k-mer is between 15 and 25 in length.

According to one embodiment of the invention, the genomic sequences of the second set of genomic sequences are regularly spaced.

The invention also relates to a system for detecting a target genomic sequence at a predetermined location in a genome of a microorganism, comprising a calculation unit configured to perform steps a and B described above. The invention also relates to a computer readable medium storing instructions for performing a method performed by a computer, the method comprising the steps a and B described above.

Brief Description of Drawings

The invention will be better understood from a reading of the following description, given by way of example only, taken in conjunction with the accompanying drawings in which like reference designators indicate like or similar elements, and in which:

Fig. 2 shows the performance and support of the model selected by cross-validation, k=21;

FIG. 3 shows selected k-mer natural capture lineage-defining mutations in a model;

FIG. 5 shows a confusion matrix obtained from predictions of all available readings (endpoint strategies) based on ONT test datasets, with or without an adaptive thresholding method;

FIG. 6 illustrates the effect of adaptive thresholds on samples misclassified using an average threshold strategy in accordance with the present invention;

Figure 7 shows these minimum sequencing depths and the performance differences achieved for each clade.

Detailed Description

A. Embodiments of the present invention were performed to detect SARS-CoV-2 virus clone complex

Now, one embodiment of the present invention is described with respect to a clonal complex to which SARS-COV-2 virus from a patient infected using a read-out generated by the ONT platform is predicted to belong.

A1 introduction to

Since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic at the end of 2019, many variants of the original SARS-CoV-2 strain have frequently appeared (van Dorp et al, 2020). Some of these variants exhibit highly altered viral properties, such as higher transmissibility and associated disease severity, or reduced effectiveness of the treatment or vaccine, or reduced performance of diagnostic tools, or failure of other public health and social measures. Thus, the monitoring and assessment of these various SARS-CoV-2 variants has become a key to managing the persistent COVID-19 pandemic (WHO, 2021). In order to prioritize global monitoring and research, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the centers for disease control and prevention (CDC) identified specific variants of interest (VOIs) and related Variants (VOCs) that pose greater risks to global public health, additional measures must be taken to prevent their transmission (WHO, 2021;CDC,2021;Parums,2021). Sequencing plays an important role in identifying SARS-CoV-2 as a causative agent of COVID-19 (Wu et al 2020), and has now become critical in understanding viral dynamics and monitoring its spread. Two main reference tools, pangolin (O' Toole et al 2021) and Nextclade (Aksamentov et al 2021), were used to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants from the assembled genome. Both of these tools focus on detecting point mutations within a variety of proteins, including spike proteins.

The next generation sequencing platform is typically used for conventional whole genome sequencing and has been successfully used for SARSCoV-2 sequencing. This includes the mainstream Illumina platform and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT). Although both techniques allow multiple samples to be sequenced together (multiplexed), illumina sequencing is still too long and costly to diagnose in time. The ONT compact instrument provides faster turn-around times by analyzing sequencing reads in real time (Magi et al, 2017). This real-time feature is critical in many clinical applications, for example for therapeutic modulation, because of the presence of SARS-CoV-2 virus, the targeted virus within the same host may silence and evade treatment. However, the error rate of ONT readings is high (e.g. R9.4 flow cell error rate of-5%), so proper bioinformatics lines are required to obtain accurate results, especially for the detection of point mutations (DELAHAYE AND Nicolas, 2021). Finally, for SARS-CoV-2, the Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) that generates amplicons has been used to amplify SARS-CoV-2 genetic material prior to sequencing library preparation. Currently, the most widely used protocol for SARS-CoV-2 sequencing is the tiling amplicon-based method (Quick et al, 2017) designed by ARTIC Network. In this approach, primer sets targeting amplicons of different lengths, typically 400-2000 bases, are designed to optimally cover the SARS-CoV-2 genome. Several primer sets have been commercialized and used for SARS-CoV-2 sequencing (Itokawa et al, 2020; tyson et al, 2020). However, depending on the primer kit used, differences in primer efficiency and amplicon yield were observed. This in turn leads to inconsistent genomic sequencing depth (Charre et al, 2020; liu et al, 2021).

The present inventors propose a robust method based on ONT sequencing that requires only a limited amount of sequencing data, enabling ultra-fast variant identification with high accuracy. This approach relies on the k-mer presentation and sparsity of the SARS-CoV-2 genome to facilitate machine learning models to identify compact genomic features that can be efficiently and accurately detected from the reads. To improve the accuracy of the model, the method of the present inventors specifically addresses the high error rate of ONT sequencing and inconsistent sequencing depth obtained using the ARTIC scheme by relying on local estimation of the sequencing depth to optimally detect k-mers embedded in the features.

A.2. data set

The study assembled two data sets. The first dataset contained the assembled SARS-CoV-2 genome from GISAID databases (Khare et al., 2021). Which is used to learn and validate machine learning models. The second dataset consisted of ONT sequencing reads and matched assembled genomes. It serves to illustrate the feasibility of predicting directly from real-time reads, without any loss of performance compared to prediction from the assembled genome.

A.2.1. Assembled genome

The heart of the method is a machine learning model trained to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants. In this work, it is considered Nextstrain nomenclature to define variants and relies on assembled genomes obtained from the GISAID database to learn and validate the model. More precisely, the method relies on a database of day 14, 5, 2021, consisting of 1:508:656 genomes, representing 13 clades. From this database, 2000 genomes were chosen for training and 2000 genomes were chosen for independent validation.

A.2.2.Ont readings

To demonstrate the feasibility of ultra-rapid identification of SARSCoV-2 variants from ONT reads, a small dataset was assembled, with 100 genomes per clade. The ONT readings are downloaded from Sequence READ ARCHIVE (SRA) and the corresponding assembly set (assemblies) is extracted from GISAID database for comparison. Neither of the genomes contained in this dataset is part of the dataset used to train and validate the machine learning model. Table 1 provides the number of assembled genomes for each clade used to train and verify the model and the number of ONT genomes (reads) used to test the model. The first column gives the clade name, followed by the total number of genomes available in the corresponding GISAID derivative, columns 2 and 3 apply to training and validating the number of genomes of the model, and column 4 applies to the set of ONT read data for testing the model.

A.3. Method of

A.3.1. Genomic sequence presentation

The method of the present inventors relies on the k-mer presentation of SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequence. DBGWAS software was used to calculate k-mer presentations as described in patent applications WO2021180771 and WO2021180768 to Jaillard et al (2020). Briefly, for a given k value, a De Bruijn graph is constructed from all the assembled sets within the training dataset. The nodes of this figure correspond to k-mers which are compressed into so-called unitig of fully conserved regions, resulting in k-mers of variable length. To further reduce dimensionality, equivalents unitig are grouped together as features. The final presentation of a given genome is obtained by encoding the binary vectors of the presence or absence of all these features and is used as input to the machine learning model.

A.3.3. prediction from an assembly set

The prediction step is simply equivalent to detecting the presence of the feature (set unitig) selected by the model in the sequencing data. To perform this operation from the assembled genome, it is necessary to perform it in three steps. Since unitig is variable in length (between 21 and 41 in this study), MUMmer was used first2018) All k-mers of length 21 are detected, then when all their constituent k-mers are detected and there is no error (no mismatch), then claim unitig is present. Finally, when multiple unitig define a given feature, all unitig are required to be present.

A.3.4. prediction from readings

The strategy for assembly-based prediction is adjusted to be able to predict directly from the readings, including a threshold for the number of occurrences of each k-mer, while leaving the rest of the procedure unchanged.

As described above, different methods may be used to define the k-mer detection threshold. The first natural strategy is to rely on a unique threshold T, defined as the fraction α of the average sequencing depth. This average sequencing depth is estimated by dividing the total number of sequenced base pairs (N bps) by the length of the reference SARS-CoV-2 genome MN908947 (equal to 29903bp, see e.g. Wu et al (2020):

However, as described in the introduction, the ARTIC protocol for SARS-CoV-2 sequencing includes an enrichment step, which results in a sequence depth that varies with genome. Furthermore, the sample composition can also lead to inconsistent sequencing depths, especially in contaminated situations.

To address this limitation, the present invention proposes an alternative strategy that relies on adaptive thresholds. This approach relies on local estimation of sequencing depth to define k-mer specific detection thresholds. For local estimation of sequencing depth, one embodiment of the present invention advantageously utilizes k-mers used by fastv software (Chen et al 2020) that aims to evaluate the quality of sequencing data using k-mers generated at regular intervals along a given genome. Thus, these fastv generated k-mers are regularly spaced along the SARS-CoV-2 genome, thus providing a natural surrogate for estimating local sequencing depth. More precisely, embodiments of the present invention proceed as follows:

1. first fastv k-mers and the k-mers involved in the model were mapped on a reference SARS-CoV-2 genome MN908947 (Wu et al 2020), and their position pos (k i) for each k-mer k i stored on the reference genome.

2. For a given window size delta, and for each k-mer k i, a neighborhood is defined according to equation 2Integrating the k-mers and fastv k-mers of the model, which are within a distance δ from k-mer k i:

Wherein the method comprises the steps of Representing the union of fastv k-mer sets and k-mer sets involved in the predictive model.

3. The local sequencing depth is estimated as the maximum number of k-mer occurrences observed within the neighborhood N i (occ), since both the fastv k-mer and the k-mer from the model can capture different mutations relative to the reference genome.

4. Finally, as shown in equation 3, a threshold T i associated with k-mer k i is defined as a fraction α of the local sequencing depth estimate. But it is worth noting that k-mers may remain isolated depending on the size of the neighborhood delta. In this case, we rely on the median of all k-mer occurrences (feature sums fastv) to estimate the local sequencing depth.

In fact, α and δ are two hyper-parameters that can be advantageously optimized to improve performance.

FIG. 1 illustrates the different steps for defining such adaptive k-mer detection thresholds based on k-mers derived from a reference genome and a model k-mer.

A.3.5. Real-time/stream analysis

Two predictive settings are advantageously considered when identifying variants from ONT readings. Endpoint settings correspond to a single prediction from all sequencing reads available at the end of a sequencing experiment, as is done in the traditional Illumina-like sequencing workflow.

However, since ONT workflow offers the possibility to process sequencing data in real time, we evaluate the added value of this unique feature of ONT sequencing by simulating the reality of generating reads in real time by a sequencer. To this end, we split the sequencing data downloaded from SRA into chunks of 1000 reads. This makes it possible to study the evolution of the predicted performance as sequencing depth and sequencing time increase.

A.4. results

A.4.1. cross validation performance

The predictive model is trained using several k values between 11 and 31. And selecting the optimal k value according to the cross verification result. The inventors observed that the k-value has little effect on the performance and support of the model. A value of 21 is chosen because of its best tradeoff in terms of performance and sparsity of the model. The total number of features involved in the model is 430. Figure 2 shows the performance and support of the model selected by cross-validation at k=21.

FIG. 3 illustrates selected k-mer natural capture lineage-defining mutations in the model. In this example, k-mers corresponding to 20J/501Y.V3 clades were mapped to the reference genome of SARS-CoV-2. This set of k-mers captures AAT at position 23063, which corresponds to the deletion of the well-known N501Y mutation in spike protein, while its presence is associated with 20J/501y.v3 clade.

A.4.2. assembly set performance

Figure 4 shows a confusion matrix obtained based on the assembled test set, each clade involving 2000 genomes. The overall accuracy of the model was 99.7%. This level of performance is very consistent with the cross-validation performance, indicating the well-generalized nature of the machine learning model and the method of detecting k-mers based on local sequencing depth of the present invention.

A.4.3. Performance based on ONT readings

By taking into account the endpoint and flow prediction strategies, ONT readings from the test dataset are processed using our prediction pipeline. For comparison, the predictive model was also tested on the corresponding assembly set from GISAID. For the adaptive thresholding method, the neighborhood size and threshold are arbitrarily set to δ=31 and α=0:5, respectively. These two super parameters are trimmed by a cross-validation procedure to obtain the appropriate performance level.

Endpoint performance: figure 5 shows the confusion matrix (endpoint strategy) obtained when predicting from all available readings based on the ONT test dataset, with or without the adaptive thresholding method. These results were compared to the confusion matrix obtained from the assembled genome (shown on the left).

The overall predictive accuracy of the assembled genome was 99:7%, indicating that this small-scale dataset represents a validated dataset whose performance levels are comparable to the assembly-based predictions.

Fig. 6 illustrates the effect of an adaptive threshold on samples that are misclassified using an average threshold strategy but correctly classified after the adaptive threshold. The figure highlights how the adaptive threshold strategy affects k-mer detection. In all three figures, the black dots correspond to fastv k-mers, while the blue dots correspond to k-mers of the model selection. The dashed orange line corresponds to the average k-mer detection threshold. In both enlarged figures, the model k-mer of this sample detected is highlighted in yellow. Red dots correspond to model k-mers detected using only the average threshold strategy. In particular, several k-mers that occur in the high sequencing depth region (shown in red, approximately position 15000) are called by the global threshold, but the end use adaptive threshold is no longer called, consistent with calls made from the corresponding assembled genome. The flow performance analysis shows that for both depth estimation methods, the predicted performance reaches a steady state defined by endpoint accuracy before the sequencing experiment ends. For the average thresholding method, the minimum depth to reach steady state is about 750×, while for the adaptive thresholding strategy, the minimum depth is about 150×. The inventors have observed that in the streaming mode, the performance obtained using the adaptive depth method is also more stable than the average depth method. To better illustrate the differences in performance and speed, we calculated the minimum sequencing depth required to reach the endpoint performance for each clade. The differences in these minimum sequencing depths and the performance achieved for each clade are given in figure 7. This result clearly shows that not only can higher performance levels be achieved by means of the adaptive depth method, but also lower sequencing depths are required to achieve endpoint performance.

From the above, it can be seen that k-mer and sparsity dependent methods facilitate machine learning models to identify SARS-CoV-2 variants directly from ONT reads. By using local sequencing depth estimation, the amount of sequencing data required for reliable detection of k-mers can be greatly reduced while maintaining comparable levels of variant identification performance as obtained from the assembled genome. In particular, this performance has been demonstrated to be achieved with average sequencing depths as low as 150 x, which may be achieved in less than one minute of sequencing time if samples are not multiplexed on an ONT flow cell. Surprisingly, not considering this local, adaptive strategy results in lower performance and a 5-fold increase in the amount of sequencing data required.

Variant identification can then be obtained within a sequencing time of a few minutes, depending on the amount of sample multiplexing. Thus, this paves the way for timely diagnosis, improving patient care in the COVID-19 pandemic setting.

A.5. Processing the readings to determine the clone complex of the Sars-CoV2 sample is a computer-implemented method, such as by a computing unit comprising one or more (micro) processors, computer memory, and RAM, and is configured to store computer-readable instructions that, when executed by the computing unit, perform the above-described calculations. The computing unit is, for example, a personal computer, a server of a cloud-based computer system, or a computing cluster. The processing results are advantageously output on a display and/or stored in a laboratory information system.

B. Other embodiments

Detection of k-mers in the genome has been described. As will be readily appreciated, the word "k-mer" represents a particular way of describing a genome, a portion thereof, or more generally a genomic sequence. Thus, k-mers are genomic sequences and thus their use in the description of the predictions above does not limit the scope of the invention;

An adaptive threshold based on local sequencing depth calculation has been described for viruses. Obviously, the method is applicable to genomes of any nature, which may be from bacteria, yeast or fungi. In particular, patent application WO2021180768 describes predicting the susceptibility of bacteria to antibiotics based on specific k-mer assays. The detection described in said application is advantageously carried out on the basis of the invention;

some specific values of the super-parameters α and δ have been described. Advantageously, as mentioned above, the hyper-parameters are part of a cross-validation technique variable and their values are selected to optimize the performance of the cross-validation;

The use of a reference genome has been described. Advantageously, a plurality of reference genomes, and preferably as many reference genomes as possible, are used to generate the reference k-mers.
